hints: Think about how much usable DNA you actually get from a single hair or a tiny trace of saliva left at a scene.
Recall what PCR is designed to do to a starting sample of DNA when you need enough to work with.
walkthrough:
Starting material is tiny**
A hair root or a trace of blood or saliva contains only a few cells, so only a minute quantity of DNA is recovered. That is far too little to cut, separate and stain to see a clear banding pattern.

PCR makes many copies**
PCR replicates that target DNA over and over in vitro. This amplification produces a large enough quantity from the tiny starting sample so a full DNA profile can then be made.
Final answer: Crime scene DNA may be present in a very small / minute quantity; PCR amplifies / replicates / copies the DNA to give enough for profiling.

hints: Think about the charge carried by the phosphate groups in the DNA backbone and which electrode that charge will be attracted to.
Think about how fragments of different length move through the pores of the gel when the same voltage is applied.
walkthrough:
Charge drives movement**
The phosphate groups give every DNA fragment an overall negative charge. When a voltage is applied across the gel, all fragments are pulled toward the positive electrode, the anode.

Size controls speed and distance**
The gel acts like a sieve. Smaller, lighter fragments slip through the pores easily and so move faster and further in a given time, while larger fragments are held back. Fragments of the same length stop together, forming a distinct band, so the set of bands is the profile.
Final answer: DNA is negatively charged so moves to the positive electrode / anode; smaller / lighter fragments move faster / further so separate into bands by size.

hints: Compare who ends up in a police DNA store with who voluntarily uploads DNA to trace ancestors.
Think about what DNA relatives share, and how a partial match could still lead police to a criminal who never gave DNA.
walkthrough:
A much wider pool of people**
A police store only holds profiles from people already convicted of or suspected of crime. GEDmatch is open to anyone interested in ancestry, so it is much larger and includes many innocent people with no reason to hide their DNA.

Relatives give the lead**
Close relatives share many alleles, so crime scene DNA can show a partial match to a relative on GEDmatch even when the criminal is not on any database. Police can then trace that family to identify the criminal and confirm with a complete profile match.

Final answer: GEDmatch database is larger than the police database; police database only covers people convicted of / suspected of crime whereas GEDmatch includes innocent people, giving partial matches to relatives that provide leads to criminals hiding their DNA.

hints: Split the word bioinformatics into bio and informatics - what type of information is being stored here and in what quantity?
Think about how thousands of genome profiles could be searched and compared to find matches - could that be done by hand?
walkthrough:
Biology on a huge scale**
GEDmatch holds DNA sequence and profile data from very large numbers of people. That store of biological information is far too large to search manually.

Informatics does the work**
Finding matching or partially matching profiles requires computer software, algorithms and statistical analysis to process, compare and retrieve data. The combination of biological data plus computer-based storage and analysis is bioinformatics.
Final answer: GEDmatch stores a large quantity of biological / DNA / genome data / information; it is held for analysis / processing by computer / software / algorithm / statistics.

hints: The rise from 1500 to 5000 uploads a day suggests many people saw a positive side - what benefit to society would make them want to help?
Think about what else you are sharing when you upload your own DNA - whose genetic information is also revealed without them agreeing?
walkthrough:
The social case for use**
Catching serious criminals makes the community safer and delivers justice, including solving very old cases. The jump in daily uploads from 1500 to 5000 suggests many citizens approved of this use and were willing to help police.

The ethical case against use**
Your DNA is also partly your relatives DNA. By uploading your profile you reveal information about parents, siblings and children who never consented to police searching. Journalists worried this stretches the original ancestry purpose and risks privacy, so use needs clear consent rules.

Final answer: Social benefit: helps police catch / imprison criminals and makes society safer, supporting justice; Ethical concern: uploading own DNA also shares relatives DNA without their consent / privacy issue. Rise in uploads suggests public support outweighs concern for many.
